terra.problem: Paul's distress does not establish that he was too bothered to admire the craftsmanship.
The text does not say Paul wasn't walking with a map or whistling, or that a disturbed person couldn't be on a relaxing walk.
The passage says Paul reasoned in the synagogue and marketplace, not that he was busy the whole time he was waiting.
Papa claims to have seen a bake sale, adding an experience outside his established world.
The passage doesn't say Paul went to the marketplace because crowds were there, or that the philosophers were among the people he met there.
The passage calls it a marketplace, not a busy shopping street.
The explanation is flat, and the line about skipping stones doesn't make a clear joke.
The passage doesn't say the listeners had never heard of Jesus or that this was why they spoke of foreign gods.
The writer gives the reason for their remark; the text doesn't say the philosophers themselves gave that reason.
The explanation asserts why Paul got a curious crowd, a connection the passage doesn't explicitly make.
Paul says God does not live in temples made by human hands, not that no human-made building can hold Him.
The joke about God's being Lord of heaven and earth as a big address makes His title the subject of humor.
The oven joke makes God's relationship to human-made temples into a comparison with a tray that won't fit.
The explanation repeats the answer and verse without explaining repentance, leaving it generic and flat.
The explanation repeats the answer without adding a meaningful explanation or Papa's personality.
It identifies the resurrection in verse 18 as the raising of the appointed Man in verse 31, though neither verse explicitly identifies the two as the same event.
The passage doesn't specify that Paul proclaimed this news in the marketplace.
The text says some mocked Paul, not that the resurrection stopped them or that they stopped listening.
A crowd splitting right down the middle implies an even division that the text doesn't give.
The last two sentences merely note that the Bible gives Damaris's name, leaving the explanation generic and flat.
